Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020
Used Methods: DT, RF, SVM/SVC, XGBoost
Core Methodology: Comprehensive survey of IDSs for Healthcare 5.0, reviewing AI-based IDS approaches, Healthcare 5.0 datasets, explainable AI (XAI), and security challenges. The paper further includes a practical case study using the WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset, comparing Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM, and XGBoost models with SHAP-based explainability to evaluate the contribution of biomedical and network features.
Major Findings: The study identifies a significant research gap in Healthcare 5.0 IDS literature where explainability, biomedical data integration, and practical validation are rarely addressed together. The case study demonstrates that combining biomedical and network features improves intrusion detection performance and that physiological data can be particularly valuable for detecting sophisticated attacks such as spoofing. SHAP explanations improve transparency and trustworthiness of IDS decisions.
Critical Limitations: The survey highlights a major shortage of publicly available Healthcare 5.0-specific datasets. Existing datasets often fail to accurately represent real-world IoMT environments, modern attack behaviors, and biomedical context. The practical validation is based on a single dataset (WUSTL-EHMS-2020), limiting generalizability. Cross-dataset validation, real clinical deployment, and lightweight IoMT-focused IDS implementations remain largely unexplored.
Future Directions: Create standardized Healthcare 5.0 IDS datasets; validate on real-world clinical environments; develop lightweight IoMT IDS models; integrate FL, XAI, edge computing, adversarial robustness, and privacy-preserving methods; establish common evaluation metrics.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant. This paper provides one of the most comprehensive Healthcare 5.0 security reviews currently available. It directly identifies future research directions involving explainable IDSs, biomedical-aware intrusion detection, IoMT-specific datasets, federated learning, and patient-centric cybersecurity. It establishes strong motivation for developing next-generation explainable and adaptive IoMT IDS frameworks.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020, ToN-IoT, N-BaIoT, CICIDS2017, Bot-IoT and other IoMT datasets
Used Methods: RF, DT, SVM, KNN, LR, MLP, LSTM, CNN, GAN, DBN, PSO-based hybrids, metaheuristic-assisted models
Core Methodology: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of 28 IoMT IDS studies (2018–2024). Papers were analyzed across AI-based IDS methods, datasets, security requirements, intrusion detection processes, and evaluation metrics. A nine-category IDS taxonomy and comprehensive IoMT security framework were developed.
Major Findings: RF is the most frequently used ML model while MLP and LSTM dominate DL-based IDS research. WUSTL-EHMS-2020 is the most widely used IoMT-specific IDS dataset. Most IDS pipelines follow preprocessing → feature selection → classification. AI significantly improves intrusion detection performance, but dataset choice strongly influences results. IoMT attacks directly impact confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA).
Critical Limitations: Lack of standardized datasets, insufficient real-world validation, limited dataset diversity, heavy dependence on testbed environments, poor reproducibility across studies, limited explainability, class imbalance issues, resource constraints of IoMT devices, and inadequate evaluation standardization.
Future Directions: Lightweight IDS architectures, federated learning, blockchain-enabled IDS, explainable AI, privacy-preserving detection, real-time edge deployment, standardized benchmarks, better evaluation protocols, and cross-dataset validation.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Extremely high relevance. Provides one of the strongest foundations for IoMT IDS taxonomy, datasets, AI methods, evaluation metrics, security requirements, and open research challenges. Essential reference for Related Work, Dataset Analysis, Research Gaps, and Future Research Opportunities sections.

Dataset: No IDS dataset used; blockchain test environment based on Hyperledger Fabric
Used Methods: Blockchain, Smart Contracts, Hyperledger Fabric, Access Control Matrix, Risk Analysis, REST API, Cryptographic Proof
Core Methodology: Proposed a blockchain-based smart healthcare architecture for secure EHR management. Introduced smart-contract-driven access control, interoperable EHR representation (JSON/XML/DOM), blockchain storage, and cybersecurity risk analysis for IoMT healthcare environments.
Major Findings: Blockchain improves confidentiality, integrity, availability, accountability, non-repudiation, and interoperability of healthcare data. Smart contracts enable secure prescription handling, access permissions, insurance verification, and EHR sharing. The architecture achieved high availability (~99.17%) in testing.
Critical Limitations: Not an IDS framework; no attack detection model; no AI/ML evaluation; no real clinical deployment; tested on a limited private blockchain environment; lacks intrusion detection performance metrics.
Future Directions: Dynamic access control, attribute-based encryption, stronger cryptographic mechanisms, larger-scale healthcare deployment, improved interoperability standards, blockchain-enabled healthcare security frameworks.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Moderate to High relevance. Although not an IDS paper, it provides strong evidence for blockchain as a trust, auditability, access-control, and secure data-sharing layer that can be integrated into future IoMT IDS architectures.

Dataset: Ember, BODMAS, PEMachineLearning
Used Methods: LightGBM, XGBoost, DNN, CNN, Autoencoder, GAN
Core Methodology: Proposed a bi-layered AI-driven malware and ransomware detection framework for SDN-enabled IoMT healthcare environments. First layer detects malware, second layer classifies ransomware. Uses static analysis (opcode, API calls, PE headers) and dynamic analysis (execution traces, grayscale malware images).
Major Findings: Bi-layered XGBoost achieved 99.60% accuracy and F1=0.9966. LightGBM achieved 99.32% accuracy and F1=0.9934. The framework improved malware and ransomware detection compared with single-layer benchmark models.
Critical Limitations: Not evaluated on real IoMT network traffic datasets. Uses malware datasets rather than IoMT IDS datasets. No explainability mechanism. No cross-dataset validation. No federated learning, privacy-preserving framework, or real healthcare deployment.
Future Directions: Lightweight deployment, XAI integration, real-world healthcare validation, blockchain integration, improved scalability, adaptive AI for emerging malware families. (Implied from discussion and identified gaps.)
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: High relevance. Combines AI, IoMT security, SDN security, malware detection, ransomware detection, GANs, Autoencoders, and layered detection architecture. Provides strong evidence supporting hybrid AI-based healthcare cybersecurity frameworks.

Dataset: CICIoT2023, Edge-IIoTset
Used Methods: Federated Learning, Deep Learning (LSTM), Blockchain, SSI, DID, VC, Trimmed Mean Aggregation
Core Methodology: Proposed SA-FLIDS, a Secure and Authenticated Federated Learning-based NIDS for smart healthcare. Integrates FL, blockchain-based Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), Decentralized Identifiers (DID), Verifiable Credentials (VC), TLS-secured communication, and Trimmed Mean aggregation to resist poisoning and Sybil attacks.
Major Findings: Achieved 100% binary classification accuracy on Edge-IIoTset and 99.12% on CICIoT2023. Demonstrated strong multiclass performance and resilience against Sybil, poisoning, eavesdropping, and data tampering attacks while preserving privacy.
Critical Limitations: Evaluated with only 10 clients; assumes IID data distribution; lacks real hospital deployment; no explainability mechanism; communication and blockchain overhead not tested at very large scale.
Future Directions: Non-IID federated learning, large-scale deployment, cross-domain IoT validation, improved scalability evaluation.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Extremely high. Directly addresses secure, privacy-preserving, blockchain-enabled FL IDS for healthcare IoMT environments and tackles major gaps identified in prior literature.

Dataset: BlueTack Dataset (Bluetooth Classic BR/EDR + BLE)
Used Methods: DNN (MLP), RF, DT, SVM, LR, NB, Isolation Forest, K-Means, LOF
Core Methodology: Proposed a decentralized multi-layer IDS deployed on healthcare edge nodes. Developed BlueTack, the first Bluetooth-specific IoMT IDS dataset, and used DNN-based intrusion detection to identify Bluetooth attacks in smart healthcare systems.
Major Findings: DNN-based IDS achieved approximately 99–99.7% accuracy and F1 scores up to 99.5% for Bluetooth attack detection. Demonstrated effective detection of DoS, DDoS, MITM, and Bluesmack attacks.
Critical Limitations: Limited attack diversity; evaluated only on Bluetooth traffic; no explainability; no federated learning; no real hospital deployment; small testbed environment.
Future Directions: Expand dataset with more attack types, integrate Wi-Fi and other protocols, detect unknown attacks, develop mitigation mechanisms, and apply data-fusion approaches.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: High. One of the earliest healthcare IoMT IDS studies focused specifically on Bluetooth communication security and introduced a novel public dataset.

Dataset: CICIoMT2024
Used Methods: CNN, Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, DNN, Random Forest
Core Methodology: Proposed a 1D CNN-based intrusion detection framework for IoMT environments. The model processes standardized network traffic features from CICIoMT2024 using two convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers to perform binary, 6-class, and 19-class attack classification.
Major Findings: CNN achieved approximately 99% accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score across binary, categorical, and multiclass classification tasks. It significantly outperformed Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, DNN, and Random Forest, particularly in 19-class attack classification.
Critical Limitations: No explainability mechanism; no cross-dataset validation; evaluated only on CICIoMT2024; possible overfitting concerns due to extremely high performance; computational cost may be challenging for resource-constrained IoMT devices; no real-world deployment evaluation.
Future Directions: Lightweight CNN architectures, edge deployment, model compression, explainable AI integration, real-time IDS implementation, improved detection of Spoofing and Recon-VulScan attacks, hybrid deep learning architectures.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant. One of the earliest IDS studies using the new CICIoMT2024 benchmark dataset and demonstrates the effectiveness of CNNs for large-scale IoMT attack classification.

Dataset: Healthcare-specific network traffic datasets for intrusion detection.
Used Methods: Machine learning-based intrusion detection frameworks, including feature selection and classification techniques to identify malicious traffic.
XAI: Emphasizes the need for "trustworthy" IDS by ensuring model interpretability and reliability in sensitive clinical environments to minimize false alarms that disrupt healthcare delivery.
Core Methodology: Proposes a framework for trustworthy intrusion detection: (1) Pre-processes network traffic data to remove noise and extract relevant features; (2) Applies advanced ML algorithms (e.g., adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems) to detect anomalies; (3) Establishes a validation protocol to ensure the IDS provides high-confidence alerts suitable for clinical triage.
Major Findings: • The proposed framework significantly enhances the detection accuracy of network intrusions while maintaining a low false-positive rate, which is critical for clinical adoption. • Trustworthy IDS models can effectively distinguish between benign network fluctuations and actual malicious activities (e.g., DoS, unauthorized access). • Automated detection reduces the manual workload of security administrators in healthcare settings.
Critical Limitations: • The system's performance is highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the training dataset. • Real-time implementation poses challenges due to the computational overhead of complex neuro-fuzzy classification models.
Future Directions: • Optimizing model parameters for real-time deployment in high-speed, 5G-enabled IoMT environments. • Investigating federated learning approaches to improve model generalizability without centralized data sharing.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by defining the criteria for "trustworthiness" in clinical security systems. It establishes that an IoMT IDS must be highly reliable and capable of minimizing false positives to ensure that security responses do not inadvertently compromise patient safety or interrupt critical medical services.

Dataset: Systematic review of 53 studies using CIC-IoMT-2024, WUSTL-EHMS-2020, ECU-IoHT, ToN-IoT, BoT-IoT, CICIDS2017/2018 and related benchmarks
Used Methods: ML, DL, Transformers, Federated Learning, Statistical Anomaly Detection
XAI: SHAP, LIME, Attention-based explanations, Dual-XAI approaches (reviewed)
Core Methodology: PRISMA-based systematic review that develops a qualitative scoring framework across seven technical criteria and synthesizes the literature around five deployment-oriented evaluation pillars: detection performance, computational efficiency, explainability, benchmarking, and generalization
Major Findings: Reported accuracies frequently exceed 95–99%, but these results often fail to translate to realistic deployment scenarios. Identifies five critical dimensions that determine real-world IoMT IDS readiness and exposes the gap between laboratory performance and operational robustness
Critical Limitations: Severe cross-dataset performance degradation (average MCC dropping from 94.63% to 29.35%); lack of standardized benchmarks; insufficient reporting of latency, memory, throughput, and model size; dependence on synthetic laboratory traffic; weak quantitative XAI validation
Future Directions: Standardized benchmarking frameworks, fixed preprocessing pipelines, mandatory computational efficiency reporting, quantitative XAI evaluation protocols, domain adaptation techniques, and cross-dataset validation standards
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Extremely high. Provides one of the strongest meta-analyses of modern IoMT IDS research and directly supports the review's central themes of performance, explainability, benchmarking, generalization, and future research opportunities

Dataset: Systematic review covering UNSW-NB15, KDD Cup 99, NSL-KDD, and related IoT cybersecurity benchmarks
Used Methods: ML, DL, Hybrid AI-based IDS approaches
Core Methodology: PRISMA-based systematic review examining AI-driven intrusion detection approaches for IoT and connected vehicle environments, proposing a taxonomy of ML/DL security architectures and attack detection strategies
Major Findings: AI-based IDS solutions consistently improve cyber-threat detection performance compared with traditional approaches. Hybrid architectures often achieve better detection accuracy by combining complementary learning mechanisms.
Critical Limitations: Heavy reliance on legacy benchmark datasets; limited automotive-specific data; lack of runtime latency, memory consumption, and edge deployment evaluation; minimal discussion of explainability and real-world deployment challenges
Future Directions: Development of domain-specific IoT/automotive datasets, lightweight edge-aware IDS models, hardware-constrained evaluation frameworks, and real-world deployment validation
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Moderate to High. Although focused on vehicular IoT rather than healthcare IoMT, it provides a useful taxonomy of AI-based IDS architectures and benchmarking practices that can inform medical IoT security research.

Dataset: Comprehensive review covering Edge-IIoTset, BoT-IoT, TON-IoT, MQTTset, healthcare cloud-edge datasets, and smart-device environments.
Used Methods: AI-driven IDS architectures, Deep Transfer Learning, Edge Intelligence Frameworks, Cloud-Edge Offloading Models, Generative AI-assisted Security Analytics.
XAI: Partial. Discusses explainability requirements and the emerging use of Generative AI/LLMs for translating network alerts into human-understandable security insights but does not implement a dedicated XAI framework.

Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Valuable for IoMT IDS research because it identifies key architectural trade-offs between detection accuracy and computational efficiency, highlights explainability challenges, and provides a roadmap for scalable AI-powered healthcare security systems operating across cloud-edge medical infrastructures.

Critical Limitations: Scalability limitations, computational overhead, constrained edge-device resources, heterogeneous medical device ecosystems, and insufficient long-term real-world validation.
Future Directions: Lightweight edge AI models, standardized RPM security benchmarks, cross-platform evaluation protocols, adaptive threat intelligence frameworks, and long-term real-world security validation studies.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Extremely High. Directly addresses security, anomaly detection, telemetry protection, and AI-enabled defense mechanisms within Remote Patient Monitoring environments, making it highly relevant to next-generation IoMT IDS development.

Dataset: Systematic review covering federated learning benchmarks, distributed network datasets, simulated medical IoT infrastructures, and decentralized anomaly detection environments.
Used Methods: Federated Learning (FL), Asynchronous FL, Blockchain-assisted FL, Decentralized Anomaly Detection, Outlier Exposure Models, Distributed Security Frameworks.
XAI: None. Focuses on privacy preservation, decentralized learning, and secure parameter aggregation rather than explainability frameworks.

Critical Limitations: Communication overhead, synchronization latency, architectural complexity, vulnerability to model poisoning, malicious client updates, and scalability challenges in large heterogeneous IoMT environments.
Future Directions: Lightweight communication-efficient aggregation strategies, robust poisoning-resistant parameter verification, secure blockchain-assisted coordination, adaptive outlier exposure methods, and resource-aware edge learning architectures.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Extremely High. Directly addresses one of the most important future directions in IoMT IDS research: privacy-preserving distributed anomaly detection without centralizing sensitive medical telemetry data.
